# Quick start

The whole workflow for human RNA-seq samples takes three steps, plus an
optional fourth. Each function is described in more detail in the rest of this
vignette.

```{r quickstart, eval = FALSE}
library(rmskProfiler)

# 1. Build the index (once per species). This downloads the GENCODE v48 GTF,
#    extracts the transcript and unique RepeatMasker TE sequences from
#    BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38, annotates the TEs, and builds a Salmon index
#    of transcripts + TEs with the genome as a decoy. Files are kept in the
#    rmskProfiler cache, the index is written to "hg38-salmon_index". Building
#    it needs ~5.5 GB of temporary space next to the index for the gentrome.
generateIndex("hg38-salmon_index", species = "Hs", threads = 12)

# 2. Quantify reads with Salmon using Gibbs sampling. This can also be done
#    outside of R (see "Quantifying reads")
salmonQuant(
    fq1 = c("sample1.R1.fq.gz", "sample2.R1.fq.gz"),
    fq2 = c("sample1.R2.fq.gz", "sample2.R2.fq.gz"),
    sample_names = c("sample1", "sample2"),
    index_dir = "hg38-salmon_index",
    out_dir = "quants",
    n_gibbs = 30,
    "--threads 12"
)

# 3. Import transcript and TE locus counts as an annotated
#    SummarizedExperiment, with counts scaled for multi-mapping uncertainty
se <- importQuants("quants", species = "Hs")

# 4. (Optional) Sum transcripts to genes and TE loci to subfamilies
aggregated <- aggregateCounts(se, species = "Hs", te_level = "subfamily")

# Inspect, locate, or remove the cached files
listResources()
```

Aggregation is not required for differential expression analysis. Both `se`
and `aggregated` are standard `SummarizedExperiment` objects that can be used
directly with Bioconductor packages for differential expression testing, such
as edgeR and limma.

# Introduction

Transposable elements (TEs) make up nearly half of the human genome, but most
of their copies are similar enough that short reads cannot be assigned to them
unambiguously. `r Biocpkg("rmskProfiler")` quantifies TEs at the level of
individual loci from RNA-seq data by:

1. building a [Salmon](https://salmon.readthedocs.io) index from GENCODE
   transcripts, the unique sequences of RepeatMasker TE loci, and the genome as
   a decoy,
2. quantifying reads against this index with Gibbs sampling, and
3. importing the quantifications as a `SummarizedExperiment` with the
   overdispersion caused by multi-mapping reads removed, annotated with the
   genomic features each TE locus overlaps.

TE loci with identical sequences cannot be told apart by any read, so they are
collapsed into a single target named by the SHA1 hash of the sequence. The
annotation records all the loci (and their RepeatMasker classifications) that
share each hash.

# Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("rmskProfiler")
```

Building the index and quantifying reads requires a recent version of
[Salmon](https://salmon.readthedocs.io/en/latest/building.html#binary-releases)
on your `PATH`. Importing and analysing quantifications does not.

# Index generation

`generateIndex()` runs the following steps, which can also be run on their
own:

- `downloadResources()` downloads the GENCODE GTF (v48 for human, M25 for
  mouse).
- `extractUniqueSeqs()` filters the UCSC RepeatMasker annotations from
  `r Biocpkg("AnnotationHub")` with `filterRmsk()`, extracts the sequence of
  each TE locus from the genome, and collapses identical sequences. By
  default, records shorter than 32 bp and those with classes "Simple_repeat",
  "Low_complexity", "Satellite", "RNA", "rRNA", "snRNA", "scRNA", "srpRNA",
  "tRNA", and "Unknown" are removed. `filterRmsk()` can also be called on its
  own to inspect the filtered records.
- `createAnnotation()` annotates each unique sequence with the exons, introns,
  UTRs, and promoters its loci overlap.
- `createGentrome()` extracts the transcript and unique TE sequences from the
  genome, writes the gentrome and decoys, and builds the Salmon index. The
  gentrome is written to a temporary file next to `index_dir` (~5.5 GB for
  human) and removed once the index is built. With `create_index = FALSE` it
  is instead saved to the cache so that the index can be built outside of R.

The genome sequence is taken from `r Biocpkg("BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38")`
or `r Biocpkg("BSgenome.Mmusculus.UCSC.mm10")`, which are installed with
rmskProfiler and whose chromosome names match the GENCODE annotations and the
UCSC RepeatMasker records. The transcript sequences extracted from it are
identical to the GENCODE transcript sequences, so neither the genome nor the
transcripts need to be downloaded. The primary chromosomes of the genome
(chr1-22, X, and Y for human) are used as the decoys.

Downloaded and generated files are stored with `r Biocpkg("BiocFileCache")`
(see [Managing cached resources](#managing-cached-resources)).

# A worked example

The package includes example data for a 1 Mb region of hg38 chr22
(chr22:37,000,000-37,999,999): the GENCODE v48 annotations of the genes in the
region, the RepeatMasker records in it, and Salmon quants of 6 simulated
samples (3 "ctrl" and 3 "trt"). `exampleCache()` creates a temporary cache
containing the example GTF in place of the GENCODE download, so every function
can be run on it by passing the cache to the `cache` argument.

## Building the annotations

```{r load}
library(rmskProfiler)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
```

A [Salmon](https://salmon.readthedocs.io) index and all relevant annotation
files can be constructed with a call to `generateIndex()`. Every primary
chromosome of the genome is used as a decoy, so building the index takes about
an hour and is not run here:

```{r generate, eval = FALSE}
generateIndex("hg38-salmon_index", species = "Hs", threads = 12)
```

Here, we run the steps that annotate the TEs of the example region:

```{r build}
# Loads the example cache and files
bfc <- exampleCache()

# This GRanges object is only used in the vignette. Keep rmsk = NULL in normal
# use
rmsk <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "rmsk-chr22.rds",
    package = "rmskProfiler"
))

extractUniqueSeqs(species = "Hs", cache = bfc, rmsk = rmsk)
createAnnotation(species = "Hs", cache = bfc)
```

`createGentrome()` would then write the decoys and build the Salmon index in
`index_dir`. With `create_index = TRUE` (the default) the gentrome is not
saved to the cache. The annotations needed to import the quants are now in
the cache (see [Managing cached resources](#managing-cached-resources)):

```{r list}
listResources(cache = bfc)
```

## Quantifying reads

Reads can be quantified against the index with `salmonQuant()`, a thin wrapper
around `salmon quant` that runs each pair of FASTQ files with automatic library
type detection and the requested number of Gibbs samples. Any other Salmon
options are passed as character strings:

```{r salmonquant, eval = FALSE}
salmonQuant(
    fq1 = c("ctrl_1.R1.fq.gz", "trt_1.R1.fq.gz"),
    fq2 = c("ctrl_1.R2.fq.gz", "trt_1.R2.fq.gz"),
    sample_names = c("ctrl_1", "trt_1"),
    index_dir = "hg38-salmon_index",
    out_dir = "quants",
    n_gibbs = 30,
    "--gcBias",
    "--seqBias",
    "--threads 12"
)
```

Quantification does not need to be done in R. Salmon can be run directly, for
example on a cluster or as part of an existing pipeline, as long as:

- the index built by `generateIndex()` or `createGentrome()` is used,
- Gibbs samples are drawn (`--numGibbsSamples`, 30 is a good default), since
  `importQuants()` uses them to estimate the overdispersion from multi-mapping
  reads, and
- each sample is written to its own subdirectory of a common directory. The
  subdirectory names become the column names of the imported object.

```{bash salmon-cli, eval = FALSE}
salmon quant \
    -i hg38-salmon_index \
    -l A \
    -1 ctrl_1.R1.fq.gz \
    -2 ctrl_1.R2.fq.gz \
    --numGibbsSamples 30 \
    --gcBias \
    --seqBias \
    -p 12 \
    -o quants/ctrl_1
```

The example quants used below were created this way from simulated reads
against the index built from the example data (see
`inst/scripts/make-example-data.R`).

## Importing quants

`importQuants()` imports Salmon quants with Gibbs samples using a version of
`edgeR::catchSalmon()`. Each count is divided by the overdispersion estimated
from the Gibbs samples, which reflects the uncertainty from reads mapping to
more than one target. The `counts` assay contains these scaled counts, which
are suitable for differential expression analysis with
`r Biocpkg("edgeR")` or `r Biocpkg("limma")`. The `orig` assay contains the
original counts, `tpms` the TPMs, and `length` the effective lengths. While the
Gibbs samples are read, `importQuants()` also sums them over the transcripts of
each gene and the TE loci of each TE subfamily, family, and class, and stores
the overdispersion of these aggregated features in
`metadata(se)$overdispersion` for use by `aggregateCounts()`.

```{r import}
se <- importQuants(exampleQuants(), species = "Hs", cache = bfc)
se
```

The `rowData` contains the annotation of transcripts and TEs. TE rows are named
by their hash and record their classification, the number of loci with that
sequence, and indicators for the features they overlap on the same strand
(e.g. `hasExonic`) or on either strand (e.g. `hasUnstrandedExonic`). The
`Ranges` column contains a `GRangesList` of the loci of each TE and the exons
of each transcript.

```{r rowdata}
rd <- rowData(se)
te <- rd[!is.na(rd$Hash), ]
head(te[, c("Subfamily", "Family", "Class", "N_Loci", "hasIntronic")])
te$Ranges[[1]]
```

## Working with SummarizedExperiment objects

`importQuants()` and `aggregateCounts()` return standard
`r Biocpkg("SummarizedExperiment")` objects, so the imported counts can be used
with any Bioconductor package or function that accepts a
`SummarizedExperiment`. Transcripts and TEs are rows like any other feature, so
they can be subset, combined with sample information in `colData`, and passed
on together:

```{r se}
colData(se)$group <- factor(sub("_.*", "", colnames(se)))
colData(se)

# Subset rows and columns as with any SummarizedExperiment
se[!is.na(rowData(se)$Hash), se$group == "trt"]
assay(se, "counts")[1:3, ]
```

For example, `r Biocpkg("edgeR")` creates a `DGEList` directly from the object
returned by `importQuants()`, keeping the annotation for transcripts and TEs,
after which the usual edgeR or limma-voom workflow applies. This is for the
transcript and TE locus counts, which are already divided by their
overdispersion. For counts aggregated with `aggregateCounts()`, see
[Recommended workflow](#recommended-workflow).

```{r edger, eval = FALSE}
library(edgeR)

# Ranges is a GRangesList that would become a list column of GRanges in
# y$genes, so remove it from a copy of the object before converting
se_dge <- se
rowData(se_dge)$Ranges <- NULL
y <- SE2DGEList(se_dge)
keep <- filterByExpr(y, group = y$samples$group)
y <- normLibSizes(y[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE])
design <- model.matrix(~group, data = y$samples)
fit <- glmQLFit(y, design)
res <- glmQLFTest(fit, coef = 2)
topTags(res)
```

The `counts` assay is scaled for multi-mapping uncertainty and is not integer
valued. Methods that model the counts as negative binomial with non-integer
counts allowed, such as edgeR and limma, are appropriate. See Baldoni et al.
([2024](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkad1167)) for details of how dividing out
the quantification uncertainty allows these counts to be analysed with edgeR.

## Filtering and aggregating

For many analyses it is useful to only keep TE loci with a single location in
the genome that do not overlap exons or UTRs on either strand, and to sum
counts to the gene and TE subfamily level:

```{r aggregate}
filtered <- subset(
    se,
    (!is.na(Hash) &
        !hasUnstrandedExonic &
        !hasUnstranded3UTR &
        !hasUnstranded5UTR &
        N_Loci == 1) |
        (!is.na(transcript_id) & gene_type == "protein_coding")
)

aggregated <- aggregateCounts(
    filtered,
    species = "Hs",
    te_level = "subfamily",
    cache = bfc
)

aggregated
head(rowData(aggregated))
```

The aggregated object has three assays, laid out like the output of
`r Biocpkg("tximeta")`:

- `counts`: the original estimated counts (the `orig` assay) summed for each
  feature. These are not divided by the overdispersion (see below).
- `abundance`: the TPMs summed for each feature.
- `length`: for genes, the average effective length of their transcripts
  weighted by their abundance in each sample, as in
  `r Biocpkg("tximport")`. For TEs, the summed effective lengths of their
  sequences averaged over samples, so that it is the same in every sample:
  TEs are not corrected for length (see below).

The `colData` and `metadata` are kept, and `metadata(aggregated)` records the
`countsFromAbundance` method used. The rows
are genes, named by their GENCODE gene ID, and TE groups, named by their
classification at the chosen `te_level` ("Subfamily:Family:Class" for
`"subfamily"`, "Family:Class" for `"family"`, the class for `"class"`, or the
hash for `"locus"`). TE sequences whose loci have more than one classification
form their own group, e.g. "AluSx,AluSx1:Alu:SINE". The `rowData` contains:

- `feature_id`: the gene ID or TE group, the same as the row names.
- `Freq`: the number of rows of the original object summed into the feature,
  i.e. the number of transcripts of a gene, or the number of unique TE
  sequences (hashes) in a TE group. Rows removed before aggregating are not
  counted.
- `gene_name`, `gene_type`: the GENCODE gene name and type. `NA` for TEs.
- `feature_length`: for genes, the total width of the gene's exons from the
  GTF after merging overlapping exons, using all of its transcripts, not only
  those kept after filtering. For TEs, the total width of all loci of every
  sequence in the group, so a sequence with several loci contributes the width
  of each of them.
- `n_loci`: for TEs, the number of genomic loci of the sequences in the group.
  `NA` for genes.
- `Overdispersion`: the overdispersion of the summed counts of the feature,
  estimated from the summed Gibbs samples. Ambiguity between the transcripts
  of a gene, or between the sequences of a TE group, cancels when they are
  summed, so this is usually smaller than the overdispersion of the individual
  transcripts. Ambiguity between features, such as between related TE
  subfamilies, remains. The overdispersions are estimated at import, so they
  include rows removed before aggregating (in the example above, TE sequences
  with several loci or overlapping exons).

### Gene counts and differential transcript usage

When transcript usage differs between samples, summed gene counts are biased
by changes in the average length of the expressed transcripts (Soneson et al.
[2015](https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.7563.2)). There are two ways to
correct for this, both from `r Biocpkg("tximport")`. By default, the summed
counts are returned with the `length` assay, which is used as an offset.
Alternatively, `counts_from_abundance` generates gene counts from abundances:
`"scaledTPM"` scales the gene TPMs up to the library size, and
`"lengthScaledTPM"` multiplies them by the average gene length over samples
first. These methods are applied to genes only. TE counts are always simple
sums of the estimated counts with no correction for length, because most TE
reads come from fragments of longer transcripts, and counts (which measure
transcribed bases) are more meaningful than abundances for them.

The `Ranges` column is not carried over to the aggregated `SummarizedExperiment` object.

## Differential expression of aggregated counts

### Recommended workflow

The recommended workflow for differential expression of genes and TE
subfamilies follows the methods of the `r Biocpkg("tximport")` and
`r Biocpkg("edgeR")` developers:

1. Quantify with Gibbs sampling (`salmonQuant(n_gibbs = 30)`). The edgeR
   User's Guide recommends enough resamples that N(B - 1) is at least about
   60, and preferably 200-300, for N samples with B resamples each.
2. Import with `importQuants()`. This reads the effective lengths and
   estimates the read assignment ambiguity (overdispersion) of every gene and
   TE group from the summed Gibbs samples.
3. Aggregate with `aggregateCounts(te_level = "subfamily")`, keeping the
   default `counts_from_abundance = "no"`. Genes are summarized as in
   `tximport::summarizeToGene()`: summed counts, summed TPMs, and the average
   transcript length weighted by abundance in each sample.
4. Create a `DGEList` with `edgeR::DGEListFromTximeta(divide = TRUE)`. This
   divides the counts by their overdispersion (Baldoni et al.
   [2024](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkad1167)) and adds the `length` assay
   as an offset. Together these are the "original counts and offset" method
   recommended by the tximport authors (Soneson et al.
   [2015](https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.7563.2)) for genes. The
   `length` of a TE group is the same in every sample, so its offset is zero
   and its counts stay simple sums.
5. Analyse as usual with `filterByExpr()`, `normLibSizes()`, `glmQLFit()`,
   and `glmQLFTest()`, or with limma's `voomLmFit()`.

```{r edger-tximeta, eval = requireNamespace("edgeR", quietly = TRUE) && utils::packageVersion("edgeR") >= "4.10.0"}
library(edgeR)

y <- DGEListFromTximeta(aggregated, divide = TRUE)
y$samples$group <- factor(sub("_.*", "", colnames(y)))
keep <- filterByExpr(y, group = y$samples$group)
y <- y[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
y <- normLibSizes(y)
design <- model.matrix(~group, data = y$samples)
fit <- glmQLFit(y, design)
res <- glmQLFTest(fit, coef = 2)
topTags(res)
```

The offset (`y$offset.prior`, the centred log of the `length` assay) is
combined with the library sizes and normalization factors by `glmQLFit()`,
`estimateDisp()`, `voomLmFit()`, and `cpm()`. The `genes` component of the
`DGEList` keeps the aggregated `rowData` and adds `AveLength` and
`Max2MinLength`, the average length over samples and the ratio of the largest
to the smallest length. Genes and TE groups are normalized and tested
together, so the library sizes and normalization factors are computed from
both.

Do not pass the aggregated counts to `SE2DGEList()` (as for the imported
counts above) or to any other method without the offset. The tximport authors
specifically advise against using summed gene counts without an offset,
because they do not correct for differential transcript usage.

### How this relates to tximport and edgeR

For genes, every step above is the method of the tximport and edgeR
developers:

- The gene `counts`, `abundance`, and `length` assays, including the lengths
  of genes without abundance in some or all samples, and the
  `"scaledTPM"` and `"lengthScaledTPM"` counts, are computed as in tximport.
- The aggregated object has the layout of `tximeta::summarizeToGene()`, so
  `edgeR::DGEListFromTximeta()` and `edgeR::DGEListFromTximport()` form the
  gene offsets exactly as they do for tximeta and tximport output.
- The overdispersions are estimated from Gibbs samples summed over the
  transcripts of each gene, in the same way as `edgeR::DGEListFromTximport()`
  estimates them from inferential replicates summed to the gene level by
  tximport.

Three choices go beyond what tximport and edgeR document, because they do
not deal with TEs:

- **Dividing at the gene level.** The tximport and edgeR documentation show
  divided counts for transcript-level analyses, and their gene-level examples
  use the default `divide = FALSE`. For genes in a standard transcriptome,
  most ambiguity is between isoforms of the same gene and cancels when they
  are summed. The rmskProfiler index also contains TE sequences, so reads can
  be ambiguous between a gene and TEs, and that ambiguity remains after
  summing. Dividing has no effect on features with an overdispersion of 1, 
  so `divide = TRUE` is recommended for genes and TE groups alike.
- **TE groups are simple sums.** TE groups are not summarized with
  tximport's methods. tximport estimates the number of transcript molecules
  of a gene, and its length offset removes the effect of changes in which
  isoforms are expressed. TE reads mostly come from fragments of longer
  transcripts, so the number of TE "molecules" is not well defined. Instead,
  the summed counts of a TE group measure its transcribed bases, and are
  analysed without a length correction, as transcripts and TE loci are in
  edgeR's transcript-level workflow. The `length` of a TE group is the same
  in every sample, so the offset formed by edgeR is exactly zero for it, and
  its counts are never generated from abundances. 
- **Moderation prior.** The overdispersions of genes and TE groups are
  moderated towards a prior estimated from both together, as edgeR does for
  all rows of an object. On data where the prior is above 1, gene
  overdispersions therefore differ slightly from those of edgeR run on genes
  alone.

Also note that the overdispersions are estimated by `importQuants()` for all
rows, so they include rows removed before aggregating (in the example above,
TE sequences with several loci or overlapping exons).

### Bias corrected counts without an offset

The other method recommended by the tximport authors is to generate gene
counts from abundances with `counts_from_abundance = "lengthScaledTPM"` (or
`"scaledTPM"`), which are then used without an offset:

```{r cfa}
scaled <- aggregateCounts(
    filtered,
    species = "Hs",
    te_level = "subfamily",
    counts_from_abundance = "lengthScaledTPM",
    cache = bfc
)
metadata(scaled)$countsFromAbundance
```

`DGEListFromTximeta(scaled, divide = TRUE)` then adds no offset for any row.
The methods are applied to genes only: the TE counts and lengths are the same
as with the default `"no"`, so TE groups are simple sums either way.

### 3' tagged RNA-seq

For 3' tagged RNA-seq, the counts have no length bias and the tximport
authors recommend summed counts without an offset. Remove the offset from the
`DGEList`:

```{r edger-3prime, eval = FALSE}
y <- DGEListFromTximeta(aggregated, divide = TRUE)
y$offset.prior <- NULL
```

### DESeq2

`r Biocpkg("DESeq2")` uses the tximport offset through
`DESeqDataSetFromTximport()`. It requires integer counts, so it cannot use
divided counts, and the read assignment ambiguity of genes and TE groups is
then ignored. The edgeR workflow above is preferred for this reason:

```{r deseq2, eval = FALSE}
txi <- list(
    abundance = assay(aggregated, "abundance"),
    counts = assay(aggregated, "counts"),
    length = assay(aggregated, "length"),
    countsFromAbundance = metadata(aggregated)$countsFromAbundance
)
coldata <- data.frame(
    group = factor(sub("_.*", "", colnames(aggregated))),
    row.names = colnames(aggregated)
)
dds <- DESeq2::DESeqDataSetFromTximport(txi, coldata, ~group)
```

# Managing cached resources

By default, files are stored in the rmskProfiler cache at
`tools::R_user_dir("rmskProfiler", which = "cache")`. A different cache can be
used by passing a path or a `BiocFileCache` object to the `cache` argument of
any function.

The cache holds three types of resources, as reported in the `type` column of
`listResources()`:

| Resource | Type | Created by | Contents | Approx. size (human) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `gtf` | download | `downloadResources()` | GENCODE annotation GTF | 65 MB |
| `annotation.txdb` | annotation | `createAnnotation()` | TxDb created from the GTF, re-used by `aggregateCounts()` | 200 MB |
| `rmsk-duplicateInfo.rds` | build | `extractUniqueSeqs()` | Table mapping each hash to its TE loci | 150 MB |
| `rmsk-rowData.rds` | build | `createAnnotation()` | Transcript and TE annotations used as the `rowData` by `importQuants()` | 400 MB |
| `rmsk-gentrome.fa.gz` | build | `createGentrome(create_index = FALSE)` | Transcripts, unique TEs, and genome for building the Salmon index outside of R. Not saved, and removed if present, when the index is built | 1.5 GB |
| `decoys.txt` | build | `createGentrome()` | Names of the decoy (genome) sequences | < 1 KB |

The genome is not stored in the cache. It is provided by the BSgenome package
for the species, and the `genome` column of `listResources()` records which
genome each build file was created from. Earlier versions of
rmskProfiler also downloaded the GENCODE genome and transcript sequences. These
are listed as `genome` and `transcripts` downloads if they are still in the
cache, are no longer used, and are removed with
`removeResources(downloads = TRUE)`. Likewise, the `rmsk.bed` and
`rmsk-unique.fa.gz` build files of earlier versions are no longer created and
are removed with `removeResources()`.

Downloads and the TxDb only depend on the species. Build resources also depend
on the `exclude` and `min_len` settings and are stored separately for each
combination of settings, identified by the `build` key in `listResources()`.
If you build the index with non-default settings, pass the same values to
`importQuants()`. The Salmon index itself is written to `index_dir` and is not
part of the cache.

```{r cache}
# Path to a cached file, e.g. to use it outside of rmskProfiler
getResource("gtf", species = "Hs", cache = bfc)

# Remove the files generated for the default build
removeResources(species = "Hs", cache = bfc)
listResources(cache = bfc)
```

# References

GK (2024). Dividing out quantification uncertainty allows efficient assessment
of differential transcript expression with edgeR. *Nucleic Acids Research*,
52(3), e13. <https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkad1167>

# Session information

```{r session}
sessionInfo()
```
